sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Colorectal Liver Metastases: Resection, TACE, and HAIC Options in China and India
sectionToMerge.intro: Colorectal cancer often spreads to the liver, and several liver-directed treatments may help selected patients. These FAQs explain resection, TACE, and HAIC options available in China and India in plain, patient-friendly language.

items.a: Colorectal liver metastases are cancer deposits in the liver that spread from an original colon or rectal cancer. The liver is the most common site where colorectal cancer travels because blood from the bowel flows through it. These tumours are still colorectal cancer, not primary liver cancer, so treatment follows colorectal principles. Management depends on the number, size, and location of liver tumours, and on overall health and specialist review.

items.q: Can colorectal cancer that has spread to the liver be treated?
items.a: Yes, colorectal cancer that has spread to the liver can often be treated, and some patients achieve long-term control. Options may include surgery to remove liver tumours, liver-directed therapies such as TACE or HAIC, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and ablation. The right combination depends on cancer stage, biomarker profile, previous treatment, liver function, and overall health, and should be discussed with a qualified oncology and liver surgery team.

items.q: What is liver resection for colorectal liver metastases?
items.a: Liver resection is surgery to remove the parts of the liver containing metastatic tumours while preserving enough healthy liver to function. It is often considered the treatment with the best chance of long-term survival when tumours can be completely removed. Eligibility depends on the number and position of tumours, remaining liver volume, and fitness for surgery. Whether resection is possible should be assessed by a specialist liver surgery team.

items.q: What is TACE and how does it treat liver metastases?
items.a: TACE, or transarterial chemoembolization, delivers chemotherapy directly into the artery feeding a liver tumour and then blocks that vessel to trap the drug and cut the tumour's blood supply. It is a minimally invasive, liver-directed option that may be considered when surgery is not suitable or to control tumours. Its role in colorectal liver metastases depends on tumour burden, liver function, and specialist review by an interventional radiology team.

items.q: What is HAIC (hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy)?
items.a: HAIC, or hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy, delivers chemotherapy drugs directly into the hepatic artery so a high concentration reaches liver tumours while limiting effects on the rest of the body. For colorectal liver metastases, it may be considered to shrink tumours or control disease, sometimes alongside systemic chemotherapy. Whether HAIC is appropriate depends on tumour distribution, liver function, prior treatment, and assessment by an experienced multidisciplinary team.

items.q: Who is eligible for liver resection for colorectal liver metastases?
items.a: Liver resection may be suitable for selected patients whose liver tumours can be completely removed while leaving enough healthy liver behind. Doctors consider the number, size, and location of metastases, liver function, overall fitness, and whether the primary colorectal cancer is controlled. Some patients who are not initially resectable may become candidates after chemotherapy shrinks the tumours. Final eligibility should be decided by a specialist liver surgery and oncology team.

items.q: What happens if the liver metastases are too large or too many to remove?
items.a: When liver metastases cannot be removed surgically, other treatments may help control the disease. These can include chemotherapy or targeted therapy to shrink tumours, and liver-directed options such as TACE, HAIC, or ablation. In some cases, shrinking the tumours may later make surgery possible. The best approach depends on tumour burden, biomarker profile, liver function, and previous treatment, and should be planned by a multidisciplinary oncology team.

items.q: How do doctors decide between resection, TACE, and HAIC?
items.a: Doctors choose between resection, TACE, and HAIC based on how many liver tumours are present, their size and location, liver function, and overall health. Resection is often preferred when complete removal is possible, while TACE and HAIC may be considered when surgery is not suitable or to control disease. The decision also depends on prior treatment and biomarker profile, and should be made by a multidisciplinary team.

items.q: What are the risks or side effects of these treatments?
items.a: Each treatment carries potential risks that vary by patient. Liver resection is major surgery and may involve bleeding, infection, or temporary liver strain. TACE can cause post-procedure fever, pain, nausea, and fatigue, sometimes called post-embolization syndrome. HAIC may cause chemotherapy-related side effects and, rarely, catheter or bile duct problems. Risks depend on liver function and overall health, and should be discussed carefully with the treating medical team.

items.q: How much does treatment for colorectal liver metastases cost in China and India?
items.a: Costs vary widely depending on the treatment chosen, hospital, and individual case, so only estimates can be given. India is often more affordable than many Western countries, and China offers advanced liver-directed procedures at varying price levels. Final cost depends on diagnosis, stage, tests, treatment protocol, number of sessions, complications, and length of stay. A personalised estimate should be obtained from the treating hospital before planning.

items.q: Are TACE and HAIC available in India?
items.a: Yes, TACE is widely available in India at major cancer and liver centres with interventional radiology services, and some specialised centres also offer hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy. Availability and experience vary between hospitals, so it is important to choose a centre with a multidisciplinary liver team. Whether these treatments are appropriate for a specific patient depends on tumour burden, liver function, prior treatment, and specialist review.

items.q: Are these treatments available in China?
items.a: Yes, China offers liver resection, TACE, and HAIC for colorectal liver metastases at large cancer hospitals and interventional oncology centres, and HAIC in particular is used at several experienced Chinese institutions. Availability, protocols, and outcomes vary between hospitals. International patients should confirm the specific centre's experience and services in advance. Suitability for any option depends on the individual case and assessment by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Can these treatments be combined with chemotherapy or targeted therapy?
items.a: Yes, liver-directed treatments are often combined with systemic chemotherapy or targeted therapy for colorectal liver metastases. For example, chemotherapy may be used before surgery to shrink tumours, and HAIC is sometimes paired with systemic treatment. Targeted drugs may be considered based on biomarker testing such as RAS and BRAF status. The right combination depends on cancer biology, previous treatment, and overall health, and should be planned by an oncology team.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for colorectal liver metastases in China and India?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials studying new drugs, combinations, and liver-directed approaches for colorectal liver metastases are conducted in both China and India. Trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, and enrolment cannot be guaranteed. Eligibility is decided after review of medical records and assessment by the trial investigator. Patients interested in trials should discuss options with their oncology team and confirm current availability at specialised centres.

items.q: What advanced options exist when surgery is not possible?
items.a: When surgery is not possible, several advanced liver-directed options may be considered to control colorectal liver metastases. These can include TACE, HAIC, radiofrequency or microwave ablation, and radioembolization, often combined with systemic chemotherapy or targeted therapy. In some patients, these approaches may shrink tumours enough to reconsider surgery later. The suitable option depends on tumour size, number, location, liver function, and detailed evaluation by a multidisciplinary team.

items.q: How can international patients access resection, TACE, or HAIC abroad?
items.a: International patients can access these treatments by first sharing their medical reports for review by a specialist centre abroad. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical evaluation, visa approval, travel fitness, and the patient's condition, none of which can be guaranteed. Planning usually involves a treatment recommendation, cost estimate, appointment scheduling, and follow-up arrangements. Final treatment decisions are made by the treating oncology team after reviewing the full clinical picture.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to plan treatment?
items.a: To plan treatment for colorectal liver metastases, doctors typically need recent imaging such as CT or MRI of the abdomen, a PET scan if available, and the colorectal cancer pathology report. Biomarker results such as RAS, BRAF, and MSI status, blood tests including liver function and tumour markers, and a summary of previous treatments are also helpful. Complete, up-to-date reports allow specialists to give a more accurate assessment and plan.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with colorectal liver metastases?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. This support is intended to guide patients through the process and does not replace evaluation by their treating doctors and hospitals.
